*Early Life and Accession*

Raymond III was born around 1140 as the eldest son of Raymond II of Tripoli and Hodierna of Jerusalem. Through his mother he was a grandson of King Baldwin II and a first cousin of Kings Baldwin III and Amalric I of Jerusalem. His father was murdered by the Assassins in 1152 when Raymond was still a minor. King Baldwin III therefore took control of the county and governed it on the boy's behalf until he reached adulthood. Raymond later married Eschiva of Bures who was the widow of Walter of Saint-Omer. Through this marriage he became Prince of Galilee and Tiberias and one of the wealthiest and most influential barons of the Kingdom of Jerusalem.

*Regent of Jerusalem*

Raymond was captured by Nur ad-Din at the Battle of Harim in 1164 together with Bohemond III of Antioch and other prominent nobles. He spent nearly a decade in captivity before being released in the early 1170s. After the death of King Amalric I in 1174 Raymond claimed the regency for the young Baldwin IV as the closest adult male relative of the leper king. Miles of Plancy briefly seized power but he was murdered and Raymond then assumed the regency which he held from 1174 to 1176. He maintained close ties with the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Komnenos and even discussed placing Tripoli under Byzantine protection. He also enjoyed unusually good relations with several Muslim rulers including the Assassins of Syria.

*Conflict with Guy of Lusignan*

Raymond fought at the Battle of Montgisard in 1177 where the young Baldwin IV won a famous victory over Saladin. He took part in further campaigns against Saladin in 1179 and 1182. He gradually emerged as the leader of the faction of old baronial families that opposed the growing influence of new courtiers around the crown. When the child king Baldwin V died in 1186 Raymond refused to attend the coronation of Sibylla and her husband Guy of Lusignan. He withdrew to Tiberias and concluded a separate truce with Saladin which outraged many crusaders. This truce allowed Muslim troops to cross his lands and it contributed to the crushing defeat of the Templars at the springs of Cresson in May 1187. Deeply alarmed by that disaster Raymond finally submitted to Guy.

*The Battle of Hattin and Death*

When Saladin launched his great invasion in 1187 Raymond joined the united army of the kingdom and commanded the vanguard at the Battle of Hattin on 4 July 1187. He had advised Guy to let Tiberias fall in order to save the army but his counsel was rejected. The crusader host was annihilated and Raymond was among the very few leaders who managed to escape the catastrophe. He fled to Tyre where he died of pleurisy in September or October 1187. He left no children and designated his godson Raymond of Antioch as his heir. His death marked the end of the direct line of the counts of Tripoli from the family of Saint-Gilles.

**The Surprising Benefits of Sleeping in a Hammock**

For most people, hammocks evoke images of tropical vacations and lazy summer afternoons. But a growing number of sleep enthusiasts have discovered that hammocks aren't just for lounging—they can actually transform the way you sleep. From improved sleep quality to relief from aches and pains, here's why you might want to consider trading your mattress for a hammock.

**Fall Asleep Faster**

Research suggests that the gentle rocking motion of a hammock can help you drift off more quickly. A study published in *Current Biology* found that participants who napped in a rocking bed fell asleep faster and entered deeper stages of sleep than those who slept in stationary beds. Scientists believe this rocking motion synchronizes brain waves in a way that promotes relaxation—possibly harkening back to the soothing sensation of being rocked as an infant.

**No Pressure Points**

Traditional mattresses create pressure on your shoulders, hips, and lower back, especially for side sleepers. Over the course of a night, this pressure can restrict circulation and cause you to toss and turn. In a properly hung hammock, your weight is distributed evenly across your entire body. Many converts report waking up without the numb arms and sore hips that plagued them on flat surfaces.

**Better Spinal Alignment**

Contrary to the common fear that hammocks cause back pain, a correctly positioned hammock can actually support the natural curve of your spine. When you lie diagonally in a hammock—as experienced users do—your body flattens out into a nearly level position, cradling your back rather than forcing it into an unnatural posture. Saggy, worn-out mattresses can't compete with this kind of adaptive support.

**Stay Cooler All Night**

One often-overlooked benefit is temperature regulation. A mattress traps heat against your body and absorbs it throughout the night, which is why so many people wake up sweaty and uncomfortable. A hammock, by contrast, allows air to circulate freely around your entire body. This makes it an excellent choice for hot climates, stuffy bedrooms, or anyone who runs warm at night.

**A Cleaner Sleep Environment**

Mattresses are notorious for collecting dust mites, dead skin cells, and allergens over time. Hammocks made of breathable fabric are far easier to clean—many can simply be tossed in the washing machine. For allergy sufferers, this can mean fewer nighttime symptoms and clearer mornings.

**Portability and Versatility**

Beyond the health benefits, hammocks are incredibly practical. They weigh only a few pounds, pack down small, and can be set up almost anywhere—between trees in your backyard, inside your home with a stand, or on a camping trip. They're also significantly cheaper than a high-quality mattress, making them a budget-friendly sleep solution.

**Give It a Try**

Transitioning to hammock sleeping does take some adjustment. Start with naps or occasional nights, learn to hang your hammock with the right amount of sag, and position yourself diagonally for a flatter lie. Whether you're chasing deeper sleep, relief from pressure points, or simply a cooler and cleaner place to rest, the humble hammock might be the upgrade your nights have been waiting for.

prompt: Write a detailed review of the movie "The Social Network". Your entire response should be in English and all lower case (no capital letters whatsoever).
response:
david fincher's "the social network," released in 2010, is a film about the founding of facebook that somehow manages to be less about a website and more about betrayal, ambition, loneliness, and the corrosive hunger for status in the digital age. adapted by aaron sorkin from ben mezrich's book "the accidental billionaires," the film takes what could have been a dry business story and turns it into a modern tragedy, complete with a protagonist who wins everything and loses everyone.

the story unfolds through two parallel deposition hearings, a structural choice that gives sorkin's rapid-fire dialogue a natural arena. mark zuckerberg, played by jesse eisenberg, is a harvard sophomore who, after being dumped by his girlfriend and nursing a bruised ego, builds a website that rates female students against each other. the stunt gets him noticed by the winklevoss twins, upper-class rowers who want him to code their social networking idea, and by his best friend eduardo saverin, who becomes his co-founder and initial financier. what follows is the creation of "thefacebook," the arrival of napster founder sean parker, a move to silicon valley, and the slow-motion unraveling of every relationship mark has, told through the lawsuits filed against him by eduardo and the twins.

eisenberg's performance is the engine of the film. his zuckerberg is not a villain in any traditional sense; he is a hyperrational, deeply wounded young man who processes rejection as intellectual superiority and treats people as variables to be optimized. eisenberg delivers sorkin's impossibly articulate dialogue at a machine-gun clip, and his physical choices, the hunched posture, the darting eyes, the refusal to blink when challenged, create a character who is fascinating precisely because he is so hard to like. the deposition scenes, where mark dismantles lawyers with condescending precision, are some of the most entertaining confrontations in the film, and yet each verbal victory costs him warmth he doesn't know he needs.

andrew garfield is the emotional heart of the movie as eduardo saverin, the friend who actually believes in loyalty and gets ground down by mark's ambition and sean parker's influence. garfield makes eduardo's hurt palpable, especially in the scene where he discovers his share of the company has been diluted to almost nothing; his stammering disbelief is devastating because it's the moment friendship officially becomes a legal matter. armie hammer, in a technical and comedic marvel, plays both winklevoss twins and gives them an unexpected dignity, while justin timberlake's sean parker is a seductive, paranoid hustler whose charisma masks a hollow core. timberlake makes parker feel like the devil at mark's shoulder, whispering that being cool is better than being liked.

sorkin's screenplay deserves its reputation as one of the great scripts of the twenty-first century. the dialogue is witty, layered, and rhythmically perfect, but more importantly, every argument in the film is really about class and belonging. harvard's final clubs, the phoenix club scene, the women who exist mostly as prizes and witnesses, the silicon valley parties versus the boston rain, all of it builds a portrait of a world obsessed with hierarchy. sorkin takes enormous liberties with the facts, inventing motivations and compressing events, and the film is better understood as a fable than a biography. whether that's a flaw depends on the viewer, but as drama, the invention works because it aims at truth rather than accuracy.

fincher's direction is characteristically controlled and precise. shot in chilly, muted tones by cinematographer jeff cronenweth, with an unusual amount of it filmed in low light, the film looks like a procedural thriller, which is exactly the right tone for a story about depositions and betrayal. fincher also stages quieter moments beautifully, like the regatta scene, shot with a tilt-shift lens to make the winklevoss twins look like toys in a privileged world, or the opening breakup conversation, a single unbroken five-minute dialogue that establishes everything we need to know about mark's inability to connect.

the score by trent reznor and atticus ross, which won an oscar, is essential to the film's mood. its icy electronic drones and the haunting cover of "in the hall of the mountain king" during the regatta give the movie a melancholy that the dialogue alone could not carry. the music insists that this is a sad story, even when the script is cracking jokes.

the film's central irony is stated outright by a young lawyer played by rashida jones: mark is not an asshole, but he tries so hard to be one. the final scene, in which mark refreshes the facebook page of the woman who dumped him, waiting for a response that may never come, is one of the great closing images in recent cinema. the man who connected half a billion people sits alone in a conference room, utterly disconnected.

the film is not flawless. its treatment of women is thin, with female characters largely reduced to rewards, groupies, or moral observers, a criticism leveled at both the film and the culture it depicts. the pacing in the middle stretch, with its ping-pong interludes and party scenes, occasionally stalls. and viewers seeking a factual account of facebook's origins will need to look elsewhere.

still, these are small complaints about a film that operates at an extraordinary level of craft. "the social network" won three academy awards, including best adapted screenplay, and was nominated for best picture and best director. a decade later it plays as prophecy, a film that understood before most of us did how social media would trade human connection for status metrics. witty, cold, and quietly heartbreaking, it remains fincher's most purely enjoyable film and sorkin's finest hour. highly recommended.

**Ten Days in Japan: A Journey I'll Never Forget**

I finally made it to Japan, and it exceeded every expectation.

Our trip began in Tokyo, where the energy is impossible to describe. We stayed in Shinjuku and spent our first night wandering through alleys of glowing izakayas, slurping ramen at a tiny counter restaurant. Watching the Shibuya Crossing at rush hour felt like witnessing controlled chaos — thousands of people flowing in perfect harmony.

But it was Kyoto that stole my heart. We visited during early spring, so plum blossoms were just starting to bloom. Walking through the Arashiyama Bamboo Grove in the morning mist felt like stepping into another world. At Fushimi Inari shrine, we hiked through thousands of vermilion torii gates winding up the mountainside. My legs ached, but the views were worth every step.

The food deserves its own paragraph. Sushi that melted in our mouths, fluffy pancakes in Harajuku, savory okonomiyaki in Osaka, and convenience store egg sandwiches that somehow tasted better than most restaurant meals back home. Yes, we cried a little at a kaiseki dinner in Gion.

A day trip to Nara brought us face to face with the famous bowing deer, who politely (and forcefully) demanded crackers. In Hakone, we soaked in an outdoor onsen surrounded by mountains, steam rising into the cold air.

What struck me most was the kindness of strangers — the woman who walked us ten minutes out of her way to our hotel, the shopkeeper who gifted us origami cranes.

Japan is a beautiful contradiction: ancient temples beside futuristic skyscrapers, serene gardens amid bustling cities. Ten days wasn't nearly enough. I'm already planning my return.

Sayonara for now, Japan — but not goodbye.

# ﻿There is a quiet revolution happening in bedrooms, backyards, and campsites around the world, and it involves trading the flat, rigid surface of a traditional mattress for a gentle, swaying curve. Sleeping in a hammock is often dismissed as a novelty reserved for lazy summer afternoons or rugged camping trips, but a growing body of anecdotal evidence and sleep science suggests that this ancient method of rest offers profound benefits for the modern sleeper. From improved spinal alignment to deeper relaxation, the case for giving hammock sleeping a serious try is stronger than you might think.

The most immediate and frequently cited benefit of hammock sleeping is the relief it provides for back pain. When you lie flat on a conventional mattress, your body’s pressure points—shoulders, hips, and heels—bear the brunt of your weight, which can lead to tossing and turning as you subconsciously seek comfort. A hammock, by contrast, cradles your body in a gentle, continuous curve. This shape distributes your weight evenly across the fabric, eliminating those concentrated pressure points. For many people, this ergonomic support mimics the natural curvature of the spine, reducing strain on the lower back and allowing muscles to fully relax. Sleepers often report waking up with less stiffness and fewer aches after just a few nights in a hammock.

Beyond physical comfort, the hammock offers a unique psychological benefit: the sensation of gentle rocking. This motion is not merely pleasant; it is deeply wired into our biology. Research on vestibular stimulation suggests that a slow, rhythmic sway can calm the nervous system, lower heart rate, and promote the transition into lighter stages of sleep. It evokes the soothing motion of a cradle, triggering a sense of safety and security that helps quiet a racing mind. In a world where stress and insomnia are epidemic, this simple, passive motion can be a powerful tool for falling asleep faster and enjoying a more restful night.

Temperature regulation is another often-overlooked advantage. Traditional mattresses, especially memory foam, can trap body heat, leading to night sweats and disrupted sleep. A hammock, suspended in the air, allows for 360-degree airflow around your body. This natural ventilation helps dissipate excess heat, keeping you cooler in warm weather and reducing the need for aggressive air conditioning. For hot sleepers or those living in humid climates, this breathability can be a game-changer, promoting a more comfortable and uninterrupted sleep cycle.

Finally, sleeping in a hammock encourages a minimalist and mindful approach to rest. It requires only a sturdy pair of trees or a simple stand, making it an accessible option for small apartments, travel, or outdoor adventures. The cocoon-like enclosure can also provide a sense of psychological comfort, blocking out peripheral distractions and creating a personal sanctuary. While it may take a few nights to adjust to the new posture and learn the art of lying on the diagonal—the key to a flat, comfortable position—the rewards are well worth the effort. Whether you are a chronic back-pain sufferer, a restless sleeper, or simply someone curious about a more natural way to rest, the hammock invites you to swing into a deeper, more restorative slumber.

prompt: Write a detailed review of the movie "The Social Network". Your entire response should be in English and all lower case (no capital letters whatsoever).
response:
## Related papers
- **The Social Network (2010): A Review**

david fincher’s the social network is less a birth-of-facebook biopic than a cold, propulsive autopsy of ambition, betrayal, and the myth of the self-made genius. written by aaron sorkin, the film crackles with overlapping dialogue that feels like a verbal prizefight, but its true subject is not code or campus life—it is the corrosion of friendship under the pressure of scale, money, and grievance.

the story unfolds through two depositions: mark zuckerberg (jesse eisenberg) is sued by his former best friend eduardo saverin (andrew garfield) and by the winklevoss twins (armie hammer, in a dual role). sorkin and fincher use this framing device not as a courtroom drama but as a memory machine, cutting between testimony and flashback with ruthless efficiency. the result is a portrait of mark as a brilliant, resentful outsider who builds a platform for connection while systematically severing every personal tie he has.

eisenberg’s performance is a masterclass in controlled hostility. his mark speaks in rapid, clipped bursts, always the smartest person in the room and always aware of it. he is not a villain in the conventional sense—he is a vacuum, a person for whom ideas matter more than people. garfield’s eduardo is the film’s emotional center, a young man whose loyalty is rewarded with dilution and humiliation. the scene in which he discovers his shares have been cannibalized is devastating precisely because garfield plays it not as rage but as wounded disbelief. justin timberlake’s sean parker is a seductive chaos agent, a silicon valley iblis who offers mark the validation he craves while accelerating his moral drift.

fincher’s direction is immaculate and icy. the film is shot in muted browns and blues, with trent reznor and atticus ross’s score providing a pulsing, synthetic heartbeat that makes even a deposition feel like a thriller. the opening scene—a rapid-fire breakup in a cambridge bar—sets the tone: mark is dumped, and within minutes he is drunk-blogging about his ex while inventing the precursor to facebook. it is a brilliant, ugly origin story, and fincher never lets us forget the ugliness.

the screenplay is sorkin at his most controlled. yes, the dialogue is stylized and impossibly witty, but here the stylization serves a purpose: it dramatizes the speed at which these people think and the cruelty that intelligence can enable. the film’s most famous line—“you’re not an asshole, mark. you’re just trying so hard to be”—lands because it is both a diagnosis and a warning.

if there is a weakness, it is the film’s near-total lack of interest in the women in mark’s world. rooney mara’s erica is a plot device more than a character, and the film’s treatment of female characters is as thin as the social network’s own early user base. but this may be intentional: the film is about a boys’ club, and its myopia is part of its critique.

the final image—mark sitting alone, sending a friend request to erica and refreshing the page—is one of the great endings of the 2010s. it is a portrait of a man who built a machine for connection and cannot use it himself. the social network is not a celebration of facebook. it is a warning about what happens when genius is untethered from empathy, and it remains one of the sharpest, saddest films about the internet age.
